topics.title: An Interesting Problem
topics.text:
So there was a wizard right? And he had 7 identical keys. So one day this wizard decides to go to a dungeon with 10 doors, and they keys can open 7 of them. But he doesn't know which key goes into which door, and worse, all the keys are identical. The wizard is not allowed to mark any of the keys, but he is allowed to know which key is which by order on keychain. Whenever the wizard walks up to a door, he inserts exactly 3 keys, and if one of them is the correct key, the door opens and the keys return to the respective spots on the keychain. But if none of the keys are correct, then the order of the keys are scrambled and returned to the keychain. For example:



He has keys ABCDEFG, and inserts ADE. The keychain now reads _BC__FG. None of A,D or E are correct, so ADE is scrambled to become DAE, and inserted back into _BC__FG, which makes DBCAEFG.



However, now the wizard does not now where keys A, D, and E are since they all look identical.



Is there a way for the wizard to open 7 of the 10 doors, such that it is impossible for the procedure to take forever?

topics.title: Paradoxes
topics.text:
So I was bored...

Again...



THE AMC8 SCORE PARADOX (what an amazing name)

Suppose that sxu is in a school with a very big math team of 100 kids, ok? After the AMC8, the coach tells the kids that exactly 50 people on the team got a perfect score. sxu is very curious about his score, so he asks the coach. The coach says no, but after sxu promises not to tell, the coach tells sxu the names of 49 other kids who got perfect scores. Now sxu is very worried because of the 51 remaining people, only 1 of them got a perfect score. sxu's chances of getting a perfect score seem very low, $\frac{1}{51}$. However, nothing the coach said changed sxu's, or any other kid's score, so how come the odds changed? In addition, since nothing is special about sxu, all of the kids have a lower chance of getting a perfect score now.



THE LEEWAY PARADOX

Simply put, you would rather take the risk with a higher quantity of leeway, even though the percentage of leeway is the same. (lol, wut?). For all you common people, which would seem easier to do, pick 9 other people, have a math-off, and win first, or finish in the top 1,000 out of 10,000 people? Another example is, would it be easier to design without a measuring instrument: a meter long pole to a millimeter accuracy, or a 200 km long highway give or take 200 meters?



THE CAT AND MOUSE PARADOX

Suppose that you have a cat, right, and the cat has cornered a mouse. The mouse ducks in a hole. Now each day, the mouse gets -1 points out of boredom. But if the mouse comes out, the cat will eat him brutally, and the mouse will get -100 points. The cat will give up and leave some arbitrary time in the future. The question is, what should be the mouse's move on day 1? At first glance, it may seem staying is the better option. After all, the mouse only gets -1 compared to a -100. However, assume the cat leaves after 100 days or more. Then the lowest possible ending score for the mouse is -100. After day 1, if the mouse decides to come out, his ending score will be less than -100 (make sense?), so by coming out, the mouse is getting the highest possible score possible. After all, since the time the cat leaves is random, chances are, it's after 100 days, not before.

topics.title: Stuck on solving these types of equations
topics.text:
So, I have just completed a Prealgebra 2 course, and I don't know much math beyond that. So when I came across these three equations:



$$xy + 2yz + 3zx = 2015xyz$$$$2xy + 3yz + zx = 2016xyz$$$$3xy + yz + 2zx = 2017xyz$$

I was asked to solve for $x$, and I didn't know how. I managed to get this:



$$xy + yz + zx = 1008xyz$$

but now I don't know what to do from there. I'd like some help on not just this equation but how to solve these equation types in general.



-Thalassic



P.S. Important NoteLike I said before,

[quote=Thalassic]I have just completed a Prealgebra 2 course, and I don't know much math beyond that.[/quote]

I'm at a very basic math level. Please keep this in mind while writing solutions!




EDIT: I've solved it; this was the answer I got.$x = \frac{3}{1007}$
 I don't need any more help (unless my answer is wrong ...) To those who helped - thank you!!!

topics.text:

Usually Rein Beau spends his day in the small stable, but when he wandered across into the large stable, Mr. Gallop was surprised to find that the average value of the ponies in each stable rose by $10,000. What is the total value of all six ponies?

The other four angles are three-digit integers which fit one digit per cell across and down into the grid on the right.
